become.gloss: To grow or turn into something, to come to be a certain way; in formal use, also to suit or be fitting for someone.

senses.head: Turn into, come to be
senses.body: The core sense, used with a noun or an adjective. It works as a linking verb, so what follows describes the subject rather than receiving an action.
examples: Kids *become* teenagers faster than their parents expect.
She *became* a US citizen last spring.
The neighborhood *has become* much quieter since the highway opened.
By 1995 the store *had become* the busiest one in town.

senses.head: Become of — happen to
senses.body: A fixed pattern, almost always in a question with *what* or *whatever*, asking about somebody's or something's fate. It never takes an ordinary subject.
examples: Whatever *became* of the family that lived next door?
No one knows what *has become* of the original blueprints.
What will *become* of the shop once she retires?

senses.head: Suit, look good on
senses.ru: быть к лицу, идти (об одежде, цвете)
senses.body: Formal and slightly old-fashioned; you will meet it in writing far more than in speech. The everyday American equivalent is *look good on*.
examples: That deep green *becomes* you.
The short haircut *became* her more than the long one ever did.
No hat she owned *had* ever *become* her so well.

senses.head: Befit, be proper for
senses.body: Formal, and most often met in the participle *becoming* or its negative in *conduct unbecoming an officer*. It says an action suits somebody's position, not their looks.
examples: He answered with a patience that *became* a man of his rank.
Such language hardly *becomes* a judge.
Her silence *had become* her better than any excuse would have.

come.gloss: To move toward the speaker or arrive; by extension, to reach a place, a time, a state, or a total, and the base of a large family of everyday phrasal verbs.

senses.head: Arrive, move toward the speaker
senses.body: The core sense. *Come* points toward the speaker or toward the place being talked about, where *go* points away from it.
examples: My parents *come* over for dinner most Sundays.
The package *came* two days early.
She *has* not *come* back from lunch yet.
We *had come* a long way for a game that got rained out.

senses.head: Happen, arrive (of a time or event)
senses.body: Used of seasons, dates, and events that arrive on their own schedule. Common in the set phrase *when the time comes*.
examples: Spring *has come* late this year.
The rains *came* three weeks after the planting.
Payday *comes* on the fifteenth.

senses.head: Come from — originate, be from
senses.body: Used both for a person's hometown or background and for the source of a thing. With people it stays in the simple present even about the distant past.
examples: Both of her grandparents *come* from Ohio.
The money *came* from a small family trust.
Most of our produce *has come* from the same two farms for years.

senses.head: Come + adjective — reach a state
senses.body: A linking use limited to a short fixed list: *come true*, *come loose*, *come undone*, *come clean*, *come free*. It is not productive — you cannot say a person *comes tired*.
examples: The screws on the handle *came* loose after one winter.
Everything she predicted *has come* true.
Wishes like that rarely *come* true.

senses.head: Come in — be available in (sizes, colors)
senses.body: Used of products and options, with the thing sold as the subject and *in* introducing the range.
examples: The jacket *comes* in four colors.
That model *came* in a diesel version until 2014.
The tables *have* always *come* in two heights.

senses.head: Come to — add up to, total
senses.body: Used for bills, totals, and sums. In the negative it often carries the idea of amounting to nothing — *the whole plan came to nothing*.
examples: The bill *came* to forty-two dollars with tip.
Repairs *have come* to more than the car is worth.
Their savings *come* to about six months of rent.

senses.head: Come to — regain consciousness
senses.body: An idiom with no object, used of someone waking from a faint or from anesthesia. Here *to* is stressed and said in full, not reduced.
examples: He *came* to on the sidewalk with a crowd around him.
She *had* not *come* to by the time the ambulance arrived.
Most patients *come* to within a few minutes.

senses.head: Come across — find by chance
senses.body: Always accidental: you cannot *come across* something you were deliberately searching for.
examples: I *came* across her old letters while cleaning the attic.
We *have come* across this bug twice this month.
You sometimes *come* across real bargains at that store.

senses.head: Come across as — give an impression
senses.body: About how a person is perceived, usually unintentionally and often wrongly. It takes an adjective or a noun phrase after *as*.
examples: He *comes* across as arrogant, but he is just shy.
Her email *came* across as far colder than she meant it.
The witness *has come* across as credible so far.

senses.head: Come up with — think of, produce
senses.body: Used of ideas, plans, names, and excuses, and also of money found on short notice.
examples: We need to *come* up with a better name.
She *came* up with the whole plan in one afternoon.
They *had come* up with the deposit by Friday.

senses.head: Come out — be released, become known
senses.body: Used of books, films, and records being published, and of facts becoming public. With no object it also means to say publicly that one is gay.
examples: The album *came* out in March.
The truth about the contract *has come* out.
New models *come* out every fall.

senses.head: Come down with — fall ill
senses.body: Only for minor catchable illnesses — a cold, the flu, a stomach bug. You do not *come down with* a broken leg.
examples: Half the office *came* down with the flu.
He *has come* down with something and is staying home.
Kids *come* down with everything their first year of school.

outrun.gloss: To run faster than someone or something, and by extension to outpace or get ahead of it.

senses.head: Run faster than, escape by running
senses.body: The literal sense, about speed on foot or on wheels. Common with animals, runners, and vehicles.
examples: A healthy deer can easily *outrun* a coyote.
She *outran* every other sprinter at the district meet.
Nobody *has outrun* a storm like that on foot.

senses.head: Outpace, exceed, get ahead of
senses.body: The figurative sense: demand outruns supply, costs outrun a budget, a rumor outruns the announcement. Also in *outrun its usefulness*, meaning to last past the point of being useful.
examples: Costs *have outrun* the budget three quarters in a row.
The rumor *outran* the official announcement by a full day.
Demand tends to *outrun* supply in the first month.

overcome.gloss: To get the better of a difficulty or an opponent; in the passive, to be completely overwhelmed by a feeling or a physical force.

senses.head: Get past, conquer (a difficulty)
senses.body: The main sense, used of fears, obstacles, addictions, and setbacks. The object is the problem itself, not a person.
examples: Good training helps recruits *overcome* their fear of heights.
She *overcame* a serious injury to make the team.
The company *has overcome* worse setbacks than this one.

senses.head: Be overcome by/with — be overwhelmed
senses.body: Passive or near-passive only, with emotions (*grief*, *emotion*, *relief*) or with smoke and fumes. The form after *be* is the participle *overcome*, never *overcame*.
examples: Two firefighters were *overcome* by smoke before the roof gave way.
Grief *had overcome* her before she finished the first sentence.
He was *overcome* with relief when the call finally came.

senses.head: Defeat (an opponent)
senses.body: Formal or literary where ordinary speech says *beat*. It is standard in sports writing about a comeback — *overcame a twelve-point deficit*.
examples: The visitors *overcame* a twelve-point deficit in the fourth quarter.
No challenger *has overcome* him in three years.
A smaller army can *overcome* a larger one on the right ground.

overrun.gloss: To spread over something and take it over, or to go past a set limit of time, money, or distance.

senses.head: Infest, swarm, take over
senses.body: Used of weeds, insects, tourists, and invading troops. Very often passive — *the place is overrun with tourists* — where *with* introduces whatever has taken over.
examples: Weeds *overrun* that empty lot every summer.
Ants *have overrun* the pantry again.
Deer *overran* the orchard as soon as the fruit started dropping.
By August the vegetable garden *had* been completely *overrun*.

senses.head: Exceed a limit (time, budget)
senses.body: Used of meetings, projects, and costs going past what was planned. The related noun in *a cost overrun* is stressed on the first syllable.
examples: The meeting *overran* its slot by twenty minutes.
The project *has overrun* its schedule twice.
Long agendas always *overrun*.

senses.head: Run past a stopping point
senses.body: Technical, mostly aviation and rail: an aircraft going off the end of a runway, or a train passing a signal it should have stopped at.
examples: The jet *overran* the runway in the rain.
Two freight trains *have overrun* that signal this year.
A wet runway makes it easy to *overrun* the stopping point.

rerun.gloss: To broadcast something a second time, or to carry out a process again from the start.

senses.head: Broadcast again (TV, radio)
senses.body: The most common American use, though the noun *a rerun* is heard even more than the verb. The noun is stressed on the first syllable, the verb on the second.
examples: The station *reruns* the pilot every holiday weekend.
Cable channels *rerun* old sitcoms all summer.
They *have rerun* that episode a dozen times.

senses.head: Carry out again (a test, a program, a vote)
senses.body: Used of experiments, computer jobs, calculations, and elections that have to be held over. Frequently passive — *the election was rerun*.
examples: We *reran* the numbers and got the same answer.
The lab *has rerun* the sample twice.
The court ordered the election to be *rerun* in three counties.
Let's *rerun* the test with a clean database.

run.gloss: To move fast on foot; also to flow, to operate or manage something, to extend in a direction, and the base of a wide family of everyday idioms.

senses.head: Move fast on foot
senses.body: The core sense, for people and animals, and the ordinary word for the sport — *run a marathon*, *run track*.
examples: I *run* two miles before work most days.
He *ran* the whole way to the station and still missed the train.
She *has run* three marathons this year.

senses.head: Manage, operate (a business, an event)
senses.body: Used of businesses, departments, meetings, and programs. Completely neutral in register and extremely common in American English.
examples: She *has run* that bakery for twelve years.
He *runs* the warehouse on the night shift.
They *ran* the whole festival on volunteers.

senses.head: Flow, leak; bleed (of dye)
senses.body: Used of water, tears, and anything liquid, and of a color bleeding in the wash. A nose that will not stop is also said to *run*.
examples: The faucet *had run* all night before anyone noticed.
Tears *ran* down his face during the whole speech.
Wash it cold or the red *runs*.

senses.head: Operate, execute (a machine, a program, a test)
senses.body: Intransitive for a machine that is working, transitive for a program, a test, or a report that somebody starts. The transitive use is the ordinary word in computing and in labs.
examples: The generator *runs* on propane.
The lab *ran* the sample twice.
We *have run* the numbers and the deal still works.

senses.head: Go on a route or schedule
senses.body: Used of buses, trains, ferries, and shuttles. The subject is the service itself, not the driver.
examples: The bus *runs* every fifteen minutes until midnight.
That ferry *ran* only in summer back then.
Trains *have run* on this line since 1904.

senses.head: Extend, stretch, go along
senses.body: Used of roads, fences, wires, cracks, and borders. Nothing actually moves; the subject simply occupies a line.
examples: A stone wall *runs* the length of the property.
The crack *ran* from the ceiling to the baseboard.
Cables *have run* under this street since the sixties.

senses.head: Continue for a period (a show, a lease)
senses.body: Used of plays, exhibits, series, leases, and offers, usually with *for* plus a length of time or *through* plus an end date.
examples: The show *ran* for six seasons.
The exhibit *runs* through Labor Day.
Our lease *has run* month to month since January.

senses.head: Run for — be a candidate
senses.body: Standard American political usage; British English says *stand for* instead. The office follows *for*.
examples: He plans to *run* for mayor next spring.
She *ran* for city council twice and lost both times.
No incumbent *has run* unopposed in this district in years.

senses.head: Run + adjective — be or become (low, late, high)
senses.ru: быть на исходе, идти с опозданием, накаляться
senses.body: A linking use with a fixed short list: *run low*, *run late*, *run high*, *run deep*, *run dry*. It reports a level or a tendency rather than any movement.
examples: Supplies *run* low by the end of the month.
Tempers *ran* high at the meeting.
The well *has run* dry twice this decade.

senses.head: Run into — meet by chance; collide with
senses.body: With a person it is an unplanned meeting; with an object or a problem it is hitting it. With a number it means reaching that amount — *costs ran into the millions*.
examples: I *ran* into my old roommate at the airport.
The truck *ran* into a guardrail.
We *have run* into the same problem every quarter.

senses.head: Run out of — use up, be exhausted
senses.body: Two shapes: the supply *runs out*, or a person *runs out of* it. Also used with time, patience, and excuses.
examples: We *ran* out of milk before breakfast.
Batteries *run* out fast in the cold.
He *had run* out of excuses by the third week.

senses.head: Run over — hit with a vehicle; go past a limit
senses.ru: переехать (машиной); затянуться, выйти за рамки времени
senses.body: One phrasal with two everyday uses: striking something with a car, and a meeting going past its allotted time. A third, *run over* a document, means to review it quickly.
examples: A car *ran* over the mailbox during the storm.
The meeting *has run* over by twenty minutes.
Let's *run* over the agenda one more time.
